_link.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of maladaptive behaviour as a criterion

toLevel2.question: What is one usefulness of maladaptive behaviour as a criterion?

options.text: It focuses on the consequences of behaviour for functioning
options.explanation: Maladaptive behaviour as a criterion assesses whether behaviour actually hinders a person's ability to function effectively.

options.text: It provides completely objective measurements
options.explanation: Judgements about maladaptive behaviour involve subjectivity, which is a limitation of this criterion.

options.text: It applies the same standard to everyone
options.explanation: What counts as maladaptive can vary depending on the assessor, so it does not apply a universal standard.

options.text: It only measures visible behaviours
options.explanation: Maladaptive behaviour considers functional consequences, not just what is visible.

toLevel2.question: What is a key limitation of using maladaptive behaviour as a criterion?

options.text: Judgements about what counts as maladaptive are subjective and can vary between assessors
options.explanation: Different assessors may interpret the same behaviour differently, leading to inconsistent conclusions.

options.text: It cannot assess any behaviour at all
options.explanation: The criterion can assess behaviour; the limitation is in the subjectivity of the judgement.

options.text: It is only used for children under five
options.explanation: Maladaptive behaviour as a criterion applies to all ages.

options.text: It requires brain scans to apply
options.explanation: This criterion involves assessing functional consequences, not neurological testing.

toLevel2.question: Why is focusing on functional consequences considered a strength of the maladaptive behaviour criterion?

options.text: Because it grounds assessment in real-world impact rather than appearance alone
options.explanation: By focusing on whether behaviour actually hinders functioning, the criterion considers real outcomes rather than how behaviour looks.

options.text: Because it eliminates all disagreement between assessors
options.explanation: Assessors can still disagree about what constitutes effective functioning.

options.text: Because functional consequences are always easy to measure
options.explanation: Functional consequences can be difficult to assess due to the subjectivity involved.

options.text: Because it replaces the need for all other criteria
options.explanation: No single criterion is sufficient on its own; multiple criteria are needed.

toLevel2.question: Why might two assessors reach different conclusions about the same behaviour using the maladaptive behaviour criterion?

options.text: Because they may have different interpretations of what counts as effective functioning
options.explanation: The definition of effective functioning is subjective, so different assessors may evaluate the same behaviour differently.

options.text: Because only one of them is trained in psychology
options.explanation: Even trained professionals can disagree due to the inherent subjectivity of the criterion.

options.text: Because maladaptive behaviour changes between morning and afternoon
options.explanation: The inconsistency is due to differing interpretations, not time of day.

options.text: Because one assessor is using a different criterion entirely
options.explanation: Both assessors can be using the same criterion but reach different conclusions due to subjectivity.

toLevel2.question: In the example of a student avoiding conversation before an exam, why do different assessors categorise the behaviour differently?

options.text: Because one sees it as maladaptive avoidance while the other sees it as a useful calming strategy
options.explanation: The same behaviour receives opposite interpretations depending on the assessor's view of what counts as adaptive coping.

options.text: Because the student is behaving differently with each assessor
options.explanation: The behaviour is the same; the difference is in how it is interpreted.

options.text: Because avoiding conversation is always maladaptive
options.explanation: Whether the behaviour is maladaptive depends on its impact on functioning, which is open to interpretation.

options.text: Because one assessor is using statistical rarity instead
options.explanation: Both are using the maladaptive behaviour criterion but interpreting it differently.

toLevel2.question: Maladaptive behaviour as a criterion focuses on the {{blank:1}} of behaviour, allowing the assessor to consider whether it is actually harmful to {{blank:2}}.
A limitation of maladaptive behaviour is that judgements about what counts as maladaptive are {{blank:1}} and can vary depending on the {{blank:2}}.
Focusing on functional consequences grounds assessment in {{blank:1}} impact rather than {{blank:2}} alone.
The maladaptive behaviour criterion provides completely objective assessments with no room for disagreement between assessors.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Judgements about what counts as maladaptive are subjective, meaning different assessors can reach different conclusions.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. The subjectivity in defining effective functioning means assessors may disagree about whether the same behaviour is maladaptive.

toLevel2.question: One strength of the maladaptive behaviour criterion is that it considers whether behaviour actually hinders a person's functioning, not just how it appears.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Correct. By focusing on real-world consequences for functioning, this criterion goes beyond surface appearances.

options.text: False
options.explanation: The criterion does focus on functional consequences, which is one of its recognised strengths.

toLevel3.question: How does the maladaptive behaviour criterion differ from criteria that focus on how behaviour appears?

options.text: It evaluates whether behaviour actually impairs functioning rather than simply looking unusual or different
options.explanation: This criterion goes beyond appearances to assess real-world impact on the person's ability to cope and function.

options.text: It ignores all observable behaviour
options.explanation: It does consider behaviour, but evaluates its consequences rather than just its appearance.

options.text: It only considers physical health outcomes
options.explanation: Functioning includes psychological, social, and daily life outcomes, not just physical health.

options.text: It is the only criterion that has no limitations
options.explanation: All criteria have limitations, including the maladaptive behaviour criterion.

toLevel3.question: Why does subjectivity in defining 'effective functioning' create a problem for this criterion?

options.text: Because two assessors could reach different conclusions about the same behaviour depending on their interpretation
options.explanation: Without an agreed definition of effective functioning, assessors may disagree, reducing consistency.

options.text: Because subjectivity makes the criterion more accurate
options.explanation: Subjectivity introduces variability in conclusions, not greater accuracy.

options.text: Because effective functioning means the same thing to everyone
options.explanation: Different people and different assessors may define effective functioning differently.

options.text: Because subjectivity only affects statistical rarity, not maladaptive behaviour
options.explanation: Subjectivity is a specific limitation of the maladaptive behaviour criterion.

toLevel3.question: How does the exam avoidance example illustrate the limitation of the maladaptive behaviour criterion?

options.text: It shows that the same behaviour can be interpreted as either maladaptive or adaptive depending on the assessor's perspective
options.explanation: One assessor sees avoidance as harmful while another sees it as a coping strategy, demonstrating the subjectivity of the criterion.

options.text: It proves that avoiding conversation is always maladaptive
options.explanation: The example specifically shows that interpretation varies, not that the behaviour is always maladaptive.

options.text: It shows that the criterion cannot be applied to exam situations
options.explanation: The criterion can be applied; the issue is the subjectivity of interpretation.

options.text: It demonstrates that only students experience maladaptive behaviour
options.explanation: The example uses a student scenario, but the principle applies to anyone.

toLevel3.question: Why is it important that this criterion considers real-world impact rather than appearance alone?

options.text: Because behaviour that looks problematic may actually be helpful, and behaviour that looks fine may actually be harmful
options.explanation: Focusing on impact prevents both over-identification of harmless behaviour and under-identification of genuinely problematic behaviour.

options.text: Because real-world impact is always easy to measure
options.explanation: Real-world impact can be difficult to assess, which is part of the subjectivity limitation.

options.text: Because appearance is never relevant to psychological assessment
options.explanation: Appearance can be relevant, but should not be the sole basis for judgement.

options.text: Because all criteria focus on real-world impact
options.explanation: Different criteria focus on different aspects; not all focus on functional consequences.

toLevel3.question: What does it mean that 'no single criterion provides a complete picture' in the context of maladaptive behaviour?

options.text: That maladaptive behaviour, despite its strengths, should be used alongside other criteria for accurate assessment
options.explanation: The subjectivity limitation means other criteria are needed to compensate and provide a fuller picture.

options.text: That maladaptive behaviour is the weakest of all criteria
options.explanation: It is not the weakest; all criteria have strengths and limitations.

options.text: That psychologists should avoid using this criterion
options.explanation: The criterion has genuine strengths and should be used, but not in isolation.

options.text: That complete pictures are impossible in psychology
options.explanation: Complete pictures are achievable by combining multiple criteria and assessment approaches.

toLevel3.question: How might an assessor's own values influence their use of the maladaptive behaviour criterion?

options.text: Their personal definition of effective functioning may bias their interpretation of whether a behaviour is maladaptive
options.explanation: An assessor's values shape what they consider functional or dysfunctional, which can introduce bias.

options.text: Assessor values have no effect on psychological assessment
options.explanation: Values can influence interpretation, especially with a subjective criterion like maladaptive behaviour.

options.text: Only untrained assessors are affected by personal values
options.explanation: Even trained professionals can be influenced by their values and perspectives.

options.text: Values only affect the cultural perspectives criterion
options.explanation: Values can affect the interpretation of multiple criteria, including maladaptive behaviour.

toLevel3.question: Behaviour that looks problematic may actually be {{blank:1}}, which is why focusing on functional {{blank:2}} is important.
Subjectivity in defining effective functioning means that two assessors could reach {{blank:1}} conclusions about the same {{blank:2}}.
An assessor's own {{blank:1}} may shape their interpretation of what counts as {{blank:2}} behaviour.
Two trained psychologists will always agree on whether a behaviour is maladaptive because they share the same training.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Even with the same training, the subjectivity of defining effective functioning means psychologists can reach different conclusions.

options.text: False
options.explanation: Correct. Subjectivity in interpretation means that trained professionals can still disagree about whether a behaviour is maladaptive.

toLevel4.question: A student regularly skips lunch to study. One teacher views this as maladaptive because the student is neglecting their health. Another teacher views it as adaptive dedication. Apply the maladaptive behaviour criterion to explain this disagreement.

options.text: Both teachers are using the same criterion but defining effective functioning differently, showing the subjectivity limitation
options.explanation: One focuses on physical health as functioning, the other on academic performance. The criterion does not specify which aspect of functioning should take priority.

options.text: One teacher is correct and the other is wrong
options.explanation: The disagreement illustrates the subjective nature of the criterion, not that one interpretation is definitively correct.

options.text: The criterion cannot be applied to eating behaviours
options.explanation: The criterion can be applied; the issue is the subjective interpretation of what constitutes effective functioning.

options.text: Both teachers should use statistical rarity instead
options.explanation: Switching criteria does not resolve the issue; all criteria have their own limitations.

toLevel4.question: A psychologist assesses a teenager who spends several hours daily on art instead of socialising. The parents consider this maladaptive. The teenager says art is their way of processing emotions. How should the psychologist apply the criterion?

options.text: Consider both perspectives and assess whether the behaviour actually impairs functioning or serves a useful purpose for the teenager
options.explanation: The psychologist should evaluate functional consequences from multiple perspectives, recognising that the behaviour may be adaptive for the individual.

options.text: Always agree with the parents because they know the teenager best
options.explanation: Parents provide one perspective, but the psychologist should assess functioning independently.

options.text: Always agree with the teenager because it is their behaviour
options.explanation: The teenager's perspective is important but must be weighed alongside other evidence of functioning.

options.text: Ignore both perspectives and use only statistical rarity
options.explanation: Multiple criteria and perspectives should be considered for an accurate assessment.

toLevel4.question: A workplace manager labels an employee's habit of working late as maladaptive, while the employee sees it as commitment. How does this scenario demonstrate the limitation of the criterion?

options.text: It shows that the same behaviour is interpreted differently depending on whose definition of effective functioning is applied
options.explanation: The manager focuses on work-life balance as functioning while the employee focuses on career dedication, illustrating the subjectivity of the criterion.

options.text: It proves that working late is always maladaptive
options.explanation: Whether working late is maladaptive depends on its actual impact on functioning, which is subjective.

options.text: It shows that the criterion only works in clinical settings
options.explanation: The criterion can be applied in any setting; the issue is interpretive subjectivity.

options.text: It demonstrates that managers cannot assess behaviour
options.explanation: The point is about interpretive differences, not about who can make assessments.

toLevel4.question: Two psychologists assess a client who avoids all social events. Psychologist A says this is maladaptive because it prevents relationship building. Psychologist B says the client functions well in their career and hobbies without socialising. How does this illustrate the criterion's limitation?

options.text: They disagree because they weigh different aspects of functioning, showing that the criterion's subjectivity allows for conflicting conclusions
options.explanation: One prioritises social functioning while the other prioritises career and personal functioning, demonstrating how subjectivity leads to different assessments.

options.text: Only Psychologist A is correct because social connections are essential
options.explanation: Both perspectives have merit; the example illustrates the subjectivity of what counts as effective functioning.

options.text: Both psychologists are wrong because the behaviour is neither adaptive nor maladaptive
options.explanation: The disagreement is the point; it shows the criterion's subjective nature.

options.text: This situation cannot occur because trained psychologists always agree
options.explanation: Trained professionals can and do disagree when applying subjective criteria.

toLevel4.question: A child's coping strategy of retreating to their room when overwhelmed is viewed as maladaptive by a school counsellor but as adaptive by the family therapist. What does this disagreement reveal about the criterion?

options.text: That different professional perspectives on what constitutes effective coping lead to different applications of the criterion
options.explanation: The school counsellor may focus on social participation while the therapist may value self-regulation, leading to different conclusions about the same behaviour.

options.text: That only one type of professional should use this criterion
options.explanation: The disagreement highlights the criterion's subjectivity, not that it should be restricted to certain professionals.

options.text: That children's behaviour cannot be assessed using this criterion
options.explanation: The criterion can assess children's behaviour; the issue is interpretive variation.

options.text: That retreating to one's room is always maladaptive
options.explanation: The disagreement shows the behaviour can be viewed as either adaptive or maladaptive depending on perspective.

toLevel4.question: How can psychologists reduce the impact of subjectivity when applying the maladaptive behaviour criterion?

options.text: By using clear definitions of functioning, gathering multiple perspectives, and combining this criterion with others
options.explanation: These strategies help standardise application and reduce individual bias.

options.text: By only using this criterion and no others
options.explanation: This would increase the impact of subjectivity, not reduce it.

options.text: By always agreeing with the client's self-assessment
options.explanation: Client perspectives are important but should be one of multiple inputs to the assessment.

options.text: By avoiding the criterion entirely because it is too subjective
options.explanation: The criterion has genuine strengths; the goal is to manage its limitations, not abandon it.

toLevel4.question: Why is it important to consider whose perspective is being used when applying the maladaptive behaviour criterion?

options.text: Because different stakeholders may define effective functioning differently, leading to different conclusions about the same behaviour
options.explanation: Parents, teachers, employers, and the individual themselves may all have different views on what constitutes effective functioning.

options.text: Because only the client's perspective matters
options.explanation: Multiple perspectives provide a more complete picture; no single perspective is sufficient.

options.text: Because perspective is only relevant to cultural perspectives, not maladaptive behaviour
options.explanation: Perspective affects the maladaptive behaviour criterion through the subjectivity of defining functioning.

options.text: Because psychologists are not allowed to have their own perspective
options.explanation: Psychologists have perspectives but should be aware of how these influence their assessments.

toLevel4.question: When a student skips lunch to study, one teacher sees it as {{blank:1}} while another sees it as adaptive, because they define {{blank:2}} functioning differently.
Psychologists can reduce the impact of subjectivity by using clear definitions, gathering {{blank:1}} perspectives, and combining this criterion with {{blank:2}}.
Different stakeholders may define effective functioning {{blank:1}}, which is why considering whose {{blank:2}} is being used matters.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the argument that the maladaptive behaviour criterion is the most useful because it focuses on real-world consequences rather than abstract standards.

options.text: While the focus on consequences is a genuine strength, the subjectivity in defining what counts as effective functioning undermines its reliability as the most useful criterion
options.explanation: Real-world focus is valuable, but the lack of an agreed standard for functioning means the criterion's conclusions can vary widely between assessors.

options.text: This argument is entirely correct because consequences are the only thing that matters
options.explanation: Consequences matter, but a criterion that is subjectively applied cannot be the most useful on its own.

options.text: This argument is wrong because consequences are irrelevant to assessment
options.explanation: Consequences are relevant; the issue is the subjectivity of the criterion, not the relevance of consequences.

options.text: The criterion has no strengths at all
options.explanation: The focus on functional consequences is a genuine and recognised strength.

toLevel5.question: Analyse how cultural differences might compound the subjectivity limitation of the maladaptive behaviour criterion.

options.text: Because different cultures define effective functioning differently, assessors from different cultural backgrounds may disagree even more on what is maladaptive
options.explanation: Cultural variation in defining functioning adds another layer of subjectivity, compounding the criterion's existing limitation.

options.text: Cultural differences have no effect on this criterion
options.explanation: Culture shapes what is considered functional, directly affecting how the criterion is applied.

options.text: Cultural differences only affect the cultural perspectives criterion
options.explanation: Cultural differences affect multiple criteria, including maladaptive behaviour, through their influence on what is considered functional.

options.text: Cultural differences eliminate the subjectivity of the criterion
options.explanation: Cultural differences increase subjectivity rather than eliminating it.

toLevel5.question: Compare the subjectivity of the maladaptive behaviour criterion with the objectivity of statistical rarity. What are the trade-offs?

options.text: Statistical rarity is objective but cannot distinguish positive from negative outcomes, while maladaptive behaviour considers impact but is vulnerable to assessor bias
options.explanation: Each approach has complementary strengths and weaknesses: objectivity versus meaningful interpretation, highlighting why both are needed.

options.text: Statistical rarity is always superior because objectivity is always better
options.explanation: Objectivity is valuable but insufficient when it cannot determine whether a behaviour is harmful.

options.text: Maladaptive behaviour is always superior because consequences matter more
options.explanation: While consequences are important, subjectivity can undermine reliability.

options.text: There are no trade-offs because both criteria are identical
options.explanation: The criteria are fundamentally different in approach and have distinct strengths and limitations.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the ethical implications of a psychological assessment system where the definition of 'effective functioning' is determined solely by the dominant cultural group.

options.text: It would systematically disadvantage individuals whose cultures define functioning differently, leading to biased and potentially harmful assessments
options.explanation: Imposing one group's definition of functioning on everyone would pathologise behaviour that is functional within other cultural frameworks.

options.text: It would be the fairest approach because consistency is most important
options.explanation: Consistency based on one group's values is not fairness; it privileges that group's perspective.

options.text: It would have no ethical implications because functioning is universal
options.explanation: Definitions of functioning vary across cultures, so a single definition would not be universally applicable.

options.text: It would only affect individuals in clinical settings
options.explanation: Definitions of functioning affect assessment in all settings, not just clinical ones.

toLevel5.question: A policy maker proposes standardising the definition of 'effective functioning' to eliminate subjectivity from the maladaptive behaviour criterion. Critically assess this proposal.

options.text: Standardisation could improve consistency but risks being culturally biased and failing to account for individual circumstances that make certain behaviours adaptive
options.explanation: A fixed definition would reduce variation between assessors but could impose inappropriate standards on diverse individuals and situations.

options.text: This would perfectly solve the subjectivity problem with no downsides
options.explanation: Standardisation introduces new problems, including cultural bias and inflexibility.

options.text: Standardisation is impossible because functioning cannot be defined
options.explanation: Functioning can be defined, but any single definition will have limitations.

options.text: This proposal would only affect research, not clinical practice
options.explanation: Standardised definitions would directly affect clinical practice and how individuals are assessed.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the strength of focusing on consequences can paradoxically lead to over-pathologising in some cases and under-pathologising in others.

options.text: Because an assessor who defines functioning narrowly may flag adaptive behaviour as maladaptive, while one who defines it broadly may overlook genuinely harmful behaviour
options.explanation: The subjectivity of what counts as functional means the criterion can err in both directions depending on the assessor's interpretation.

options.text: Because the criterion always leads to over-pathologising
options.explanation: The direction of error depends on the assessor's interpretation, not a fixed tendency.

options.text: Because consequences are irrelevant to assessment
options.explanation: Consequences are relevant; the issue is how they are interpreted.

options.text: This paradox does not exist in practice
options.explanation: This is a well-recognised issue in the application of the criterion.

toLevel5.question: Critically assess how power dynamics between an assessor and client might affect the application of the maladaptive behaviour criterion.

options.text: The assessor's definition of functioning may be imposed on the client, whose own understanding of their behaviour may be undervalued due to the power imbalance
options.explanation: Power dynamics can lead to the assessor's perspective dominating, potentially misclassifying behaviour that the client views as adaptive.

options.text: Power dynamics are irrelevant to psychological assessment
options.explanation: Power dynamics are widely recognised as influencing assessment processes and outcomes.

options.text: Clients always have more power than assessors
options.explanation: In assessment contexts, the assessor typically holds more interpretive power.

options.text: Power dynamics only affect the cultural perspectives criterion
options.explanation: Power dynamics affect multiple aspects of assessment, including how the maladaptive behaviour criterion is applied.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate whether combining the maladaptive behaviour criterion with statistical rarity and personal distress could effectively overcome each criterion's individual limitations.

options.text: Combining them compensates for individual weaknesses but does not eliminate limitations entirely, as subjectivity, concealment, and value-blindness of rarity still need careful management
options.explanation: Multiple criteria reduce the impact of any single limitation, but each still contributes its challenges, requiring thoughtful integration.

options.text: Combining criteria completely eliminates all limitations
options.explanation: Combination helps but does not eliminate limitations; each criterion still has inherent challenges.

options.text: Combining criteria creates more problems than it solves
options.explanation: Combination generally improves assessment quality, even though it does not eliminate all challenges.

options.text: The criteria cannot be used together because they are contradictory
options.explanation: The criteria complement each other by addressing different aspects of behaviour.
